title: Encrypted Channel: Asymmetric Cryptography
summary: This sub-technique covers command and control traffic that uses a public key algorithm, where each party holds a key pair made of one public key and one private key. The sender encrypts with the receiver's public key, and only the matching private key can decrypt, so the operator can distribute a key openly without giving away the ability to read messages. Common algorithms here are RSA and ElGamal. Public key operations are much slower than symmetric ones, so most real protocols use them only to agree on or deliver a session key and then switch to a symmetric cipher for the bulk of the data; because that handshake is asymmetric, the technique is classified in this branch. Traffic protected this way is usually indistinguishable from ordinary TLS (Transport Layer Security) at the packet level, so defenders work from process behaviour, certificate details, destination reputation, and the presence of encrypted sessions from hosts that should not be starting them.

beginner.definition: Asymmetric encryption uses two keys, called a key pair. One key is public and can be shared with anyone, while the other stays private. A message locked with the public key can only be opened with the private key. This sub-technique covers the Encrypted Channel parent when a key pair is used.
beginner.whyItMatters: Public key methods let the attacker share a key safely over the internet. Even if you capture the traffic, you cannot decrypt it without the private key. You also cannot tell it apart from normal secure web traffic by looking at the bytes. That makes detection harder and slower. Teams must rely on behaviour and context instead of content.
howItWorks: Each side creates a key pair, with one public key and one private key.
The public key travels openly, while the private key is never shared.
The sender encrypts its message using the receiver's openly shared public key.
Only the matching private key on the other side can decrypt that message.
Because this method is slow, most protocols use it to agree on a session key.
After the handshake, faster symmetric encryption carries the rest of the data.
beginner.example: Imagine a post box with a padlock that anyone can close but only one person can open. The owner hands out open padlocks to friends. A friend puts a letter in a box and snaps the padlock shut. Only the owner's key can open it again. Asymmetric encryption works like this. Publishing the open padlock is safe. The danger starts when the private key is stolen or the owner is not who they claim to be.
takeaways: A key pair has a public part that is shared and a private part that is not.
Encrypting with the public key protects data for the holder of the private key.
Most secure sessions use a key pair first and a shared key afterwards.

objectives: Define asymmetric cryptography and explain the role of each key in the pair.
Explain why this sub-technique differs from the symmetric branch of the parent.
Describe why protocols mix a key pair handshake with faster symmetric ciphers.
Explain what a defender can still observe in this kind of encrypted session.
Recognise why this traffic resembles legitimate secure web traffic.
